# Nūr: the About page and the blog, in full

> Nūr teaches you Islam through the Quran: read it, memorise it, listen to its stories, and put good manners into practice every day.


---

# About Nūr

URL: https://getnurapp.com/en/about/
Language: en

Nūr teaches you Islam through the Quran: read it, memorise it, listen to its stories, and put good manners into practice every day. Here’s what you need to know, in ten questions.

## What is Nūr?

Nūr is an app for iPhone and Android. It teaches you to read the Quran from the very first letter, then to memorise it, one surah at a time. It also tells you the stories of the prophets and companions, and helps you put everyday good manners into practice.

## Do I need to read Arabic already?

No. Nūr starts at the first letter: the letters, then joined letters, the vowel marks, and finally the page of the Quran. If you can already read, you start straight with memorising.

## How does Nūr help me memorise?

You hear each passage recited by Shaykh Maḥmūd Khalīl al-Ḥuṣarī, read it along with him, then on your own, and recite it from memory. Your phone listens to your recitation and checks every word. Each day, a revision brings back what you’ve learned, so it stays with you.

The path runs from al-Fātiḥah through Juzʾ ʿAmma, then on until it covers the whole Quran.

## Where do the stories come from?

From the Quran and from authenticated reports. Each story is told aloud, on large illustrated pages.

## Who is Nūr for?

Nūr is made for teenagers and adults who want to learn Islam through the Quran: someone who can’t read a letter yet, someone who reads and wants to memorise, and someone who wants the stories and the manners. Several people in one household can learn with a single account.

## How much does Nūr cost?

Nūr works by subscription. You choose a yearly plan with a 7-day free trial, or a monthly plan with no trial. The price is shown on the App Store and Google Play, for your country.

## Which languages does Nūr speak?

French and English. The Quran is in Arabic, with its complete text.

## What data does Nūr keep?

Nūr works without an account. Without one, we hold nothing about you. Recordings of your voice never leave your phone. There are no ads and no advertising ID, and you can delete everything from inside the app. The details are in the privacy policy.

## Who makes Nūr?

Nūr is created and published by Ahmed. The legal notice has the details.

## Where can I get Nūr?

On the App Store and Google Play.

# À propos de Nūr

URL: https://getnurapp.com/a-propos/
Language: fr

Nūr t’apprend l’islam à partir du Coran : le lire, le mémoriser, écouter ses histoires et pratiquer les bonnes manières au quotidien. Voici l’essentiel, en dix questions.

## Qu’est-ce que Nūr ?

Nūr est une appli pour iPhone et Android. Elle t’apprend à lire le Coran depuis la première lettre, puis à le mémoriser, sourate après sourate. Elle te raconte aussi les histoires des prophètes et des compagnons, et te fait pratiquer les bonnes manières du quotidien.

## Faut-il déjà savoir lire l’arabe ?

Non. Nūr commence à la première lettre : les lettres, puis les lettres liées, les signes, et enfin la page du Coran. Si tu lis déjà, tu commences directement par la mémorisation.

## Comment Nūr aide-t-il à mémoriser ?

Tu écoutes chaque passage récité par cheikh Maḥmūd Khalīl al-Ḥuṣarī, tu le lis avec lui, puis seul, et tu le récites de mémoire. Ton téléphone écoute ta récitation et vérifie chaque mot. Chaque jour, une révision fait revenir ce que tu as appris, pour que tu le gardes.

Le parcours va d’al-Fātiḥa à Juzʾ ʿAmma, puis continue jusqu’à couvrir tout le Coran.

## D’où viennent les histoires ?

Du Coran et de récits authentifiés. Chaque histoire est racontée à voix haute, sur de grandes pages illustrées.

## Pour qui est Nūr ?

Nūr s’adresse aux adolescents et aux adultes qui veulent apprendre l’islam à partir du Coran : à celui qui ne lit pas encore une lettre, à celui qui lit et veut mémoriser, et à celui qui veut les histoires et les bonnes manières. Plusieurs personnes d’un même foyer peuvent apprendre avec un seul compte.

## Combien coûte Nūr ?

Nūr fonctionne par abonnement. Tu choisis un abonnement annuel, avec 7 jours d’essai gratuits, ou un abonnement mensuel, sans essai. Le prix s’affiche dans l’App Store et sur Google Play, selon ton pays.

## Dans quelles langues ?

En français et en anglais. Le Coran est en arabe, avec son texte complet.

## Quelles données Nūr garde-t-il ?

Nūr fonctionne sans compte. Sans compte, nous ne détenons rien sur toi. Les enregistrements de ta voix ne quittent jamais ton téléphone. Il n’y a ni publicité ni identifiant publicitaire, et tu peux tout effacer depuis l’appli. Le détail est dans la politique de confidentialité.

## Qui fait Nūr ?

Nūr est créé et édité par Ahmed. Les mentions légales donnent les détails.

## Où télécharger Nūr ?

Sur l’App Store et Google Play.

# How to Memorise a Surah Fast and Keep It

URL: https://getnurapp.com/en/blog/how-to-memorize-a-surah-fast/
Language: en

To learn a surah quickly, break it into short passages. Listen to each passage being recited, read it yourself, then recite it from memory. Most of the time you save comes later: revise a surah the next day and you won’t have to learn it all over again.

## Should you listen to a surah before you learn it?

Yes, and more than once. Start by listening to the whole surah with the text in front of you. Your ear picks up the rhythm, the pauses and the sound of each word before you say any of them.

Choose one reciter and stick with him. You’ll hear the same melody every time, and that melody helps you remember the order of the words. Go for a slow recitation where every sound is clear, such as Shaykh Maḥmūd Khalīl al-Ḥuṣarī’s.

Can’t read Arabic yet? You can still learn a short surah by ear, by listening and repeating. Learning to read will help you later with longer surahs.

## How many verses should you learn in one session?

Start with about three verses, or roughly fifty words. That’s the most common passage size in Nūr, which divides the whole Quran into 1,710 passages.

Count the words too, because verses vary a lot in length. The three verses of al-Kawthar come to ten words in total. Verse 282 of al-Baqarah has 128 words on its own.

Take each passage through these four steps:

- Listen to it two or three times, following the text.
- Read along with the reciter , word by word.
- Read it on your own , out loud, without the audio.
- Recite it from memory , then check it against the text.Once a passage has stuck, add the next one. If it won’t stick, split it in two. The right size is whatever you can recite from memory by the end of the session.

## Can you learn a surah in one day?

For a short surah, yes. Al-Ikhlāṣ has four verses and fifteen words, so one or two sessions may be enough. A long surah is another matter. Al-Kahf has 110 verses and takes several weeks.

The real test comes the next day. A surah you learn in an hour and then leave alone soon fades. Recite it again the next day, and again the week after, and it stays with you.

The Quran itself speaks of this ease. In Surah al-Qamar, Allah says: وَلَقَدۡ يَسَّرۡنَا ٱلۡقُرۡءَانَ لِلذِّكۡرِ فَهَلۡ مِن مُّدَّكِرࣲ‏ (54:17). It means: “We have made the Quran easy to remember. Is there anyone who will remember?” The same sentence appears four times in that surah.

> The real test comes the next day.

## Learning a long surah like al-Kahf or Yā-Sīn

Learn a long surah as a series of short ones. Split it into passages that follow the meaning, for example where a story begins. Al-Kahf has 110 verses, so passages of three or four verses come to about thirty sessions. Yā-Sīn (Yaseen) has 83 shorter verses, so passages of five or six come to about fifteen.

Each day, start by reciting the passages from previous days, then add today’s. Always link the new passage to the one before it: recite the end of one and the start of the next without stopping. Memory most often gets stuck where two passages meet.

A long surah takes effort, and that effort counts. The Prophet ﷺ said that someone who recites the Quran with ease is with the noble and righteous angels. And someone who recites it with difficulty, stumbling over the words, gets two rewards (reported by al-Bukhārī, no. 4937, and Muslim, no. 798).

## How to avoid forgetting a surah you learned quickly

Revise it at longer and longer intervals: the next day, three days later, a week later, then a month later. Each time, recite it from memory before you look at the text. The effort of remembering is what makes it stick. If a passage has slipped, revise it sooner next time.

The Prophet ﷺ told people to keep returning to the Quran, because it slips away faster than camels slip free of their hobbles. Al-Bukhārī (no. 5033) and Muslim (no. 791) both report it. It’s a practical image: a camel you keep an eye on stays put.

For the full method, and how long the whole Quran takes, see How to Memorise the Quran Without Forgetting It.

## Do you need to understand the meaning of the verses?

Not to start with. But the meaning helps a great deal when it comes to remembering. When you know what a passage says, you know what comes next, so the rest comes back to you more easily.

Before you learn a passage, read what it means in your own language. A sentence or two is enough. You don’t need to speak Arabic for that.

Stories help too. Al-Kahf tells of young men who took refuge in a cave, where Allah made them sleep for years. Al-Fīl tells of an army that came with an elephant, and of how Allah stopped it. Once you know the story, you can follow the surah as it unfolds.

In Nūr, the Memorise section takes you through these four steps with al-Ḥuṣarī’s recitation, and Nūr listens to every word as you recite from memory.

# Juz Amma Surah List in Order, and Where to Start

URL: https://getnurapp.com/en/blog/juz-amma-surah-list/
Language: en

Juz Amma has 37 surahs. It opens with an-Naba, surah 78, and ends with an-Nās, surah 114, the last surah of the Quran. Below you'll find the full list in order, with the meaning of each name, and where to start if you want to memorise them.

## What is Juz Amma?

The Quran is divided into 30 parts of roughly equal length. In Arabic, each part is called a juzʾ, usually written "juz" in English. Juz Amma is the thirtieth and last of them, so it's also known as juz 30.

It's named after its first word, ʿamma, which opens Surah an-Naba: عَمَّ يَتَسَآءَلُونَ. It means: "What are they asking one another about?"

Most of its surahs are short, and they're where many people start memorising the Quran.

## How many surahs are in Juz Amma?

Juz Amma contains **37 surahs** and 564 verses. It starts at the very beginning of an-Naba, so none of its surahs is split between two parts.

The longest is an-Nāziʿāt, with 46 verses. The shortest have just three each: al-ʿAṣr, al-Kawthar and an-Naṣr.

## The 37 surahs of Juz Amma, in order

The number shows where the surah sits in the Quran. The "Meaning" column translates the surah's name, not its text.

| No. | Arabic | Name | Meaning | Verses |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 78 | سُوْرَةُ النَّبَاِ | An-Naba | The News | 40 |
| 79 | سُوْرَةُ النَّازِعَاتِ | An-Nāziʿāt | Those Who Tear Out | 46 |
| 80 | سُوْرَةُ عَبَسَ | ʿAbasa | He Frowned | 42 |
| 81 | سُوْرَةُ التَّكْوِيْرِ | At-Takwīr | The Folding Up | 29 |
| 82 | سُوْرَةُ الْاِنْفِطَارِ | Al-Infiṭār | The Splitting Open | 19 |
| 83 | سُوْرَةُ المُطَفِّفِيْنَ | Al-Muṭaffifīn | Those Who Cheat | 36 |
| 84 | سُوْرَةُ الاِنْشِقَاقِ | Al-Inshiqāq | The Tearing Apart | 25 |
| 85 | سُوْرَةُ الْبُرُوْجِ | Al-Burūj | The Constellations | 22 |
| 86 | سُوْرَةُ الطَّارِقِ | Aṭ-Ṭāriq | The Night Star | 17 |
| 87 | سُوْرَةُ الْاَعْلٰي | Al-Aʿlā | The Most High | 19 |
| 88 | سُوْرَةُ الْغَاشِيَةِ | Al-Ghāshiyah | The Overwhelming Event | 26 |
| 89 | سُوْرَةُ الْفَجْرِ | Al-Fajr | The Dawn | 30 |
| 90 | سُوْرَةُ الْبَلَدِ | Al-Balad | The City | 20 |
| 91 | سُوْرَةُ الشَّمْسِ | Ash-Shams | The Sun | 15 |
| 92 | سُوْرَةُ الَّيْلِ | Al-Layl | The Night | 21 |
| 93 | سُوْرَةُ الضُّحٰي | Aḍ-Ḍuḥā | The Morning Light | 11 |
| 94 | سُوْرَةُ الشَّرْحِ | Ash-Sharḥ | The Relief | 8 |
| 95 | سُوْرَةُ التِّيْنِ | At-Tīn | The Fig | 8 |
| 96 | سُوْرَةُ الْعَلَقِ | Al-ʿAlaq | The Clinging Clot | 19 |
| 97 | سُوْرَةُ الْقَدْرِ | Al-Qadr | The Decree | 5 |
| 98 | سُوْرَةُ الْبَيِّنَةِ | Al-Bayyinah | The Clear Proof | 8 |
| 99 | سُوْرَةُ الزِّلْزَالِ | Az-Zalzalah | The Earthquake | 8 |
| 100 | سُوْرَةُ العٰدِيٰتِ | Al-ʿĀdiyāt | The Charging Horses | 11 |
| 101 | سُوْرَةُ الْقَارِعَةِ | Al-Qāriʿah | The Striking Calamity | 11 |
| 102 | سُوْرَةُ التَّكَاثُرِ | At-Takāthur | Competing for More | 8 |
| 103 | سُوْرَةُ الْعَصْرِ | Al-ʿAṣr | Time | 3 |
| 104 | سُوْرَةُ الْهُمَزَةِ | Al-Humazah | The Slanderer | 9 |
| 105 | سُوْرَةُ الْفِيْلِ | Al-Fīl | The Elephant | 5 |
| 106 | سُوْرَةُ قُرَيْشٍ | Quraysh | Quraysh | 4 |
| 107 | سُوْرَةُ الْمَاعُوْنِ | Al-Māʿūn | Small Kindnesses | 7 |
| 108 | سُوْرَةُ الْكَوْثَرِ | Al-Kawthar | Abundance | 3 |
| 109 | سُوْرَةُ الْكَافِرُوْنَ | Al-Kāfirūn | The Disbelievers | 6 |
| 110 | سُوْرَةُ النَّصْرِ | An-Naṣr | The Help | 3 |
| 111 | سُوْرَةُ المَسَدِ | Al-Masad | The Palm Fibre | 5 |
| 112 | سُوْرَةُ الْاِخْلَاصِ | Al-Ikhlāṣ | Sincerity | 4 |
| 113 | سُوْرَةُ الْفَلَقِ | Al-Falaq | The Daybreak | 5 |
| 114 | سُوْرَةُ النَّاسِ | An-Nās | Mankind | 6 |

The names use Nūr's spelling. You'll also see them written in plain letters, such as An-Nas, Al-Ikhlas or Ad-Duha.

## How many hizb are in Juz Amma?

Two. A hizb is half a juzʾ, and the Quran has 60 of them. Juz Amma covers the last two: the 59th and the 60th.

- Hizb 59 begins with an-Naba (78) and ends with aṭ-Ṭāriq (86). It has 276 verses.
- Hizb 60 begins with al-Aʿlā (87) and ends with an-Nās (114). It has 288 verses.The second hizb has more surahs, 28 compared with 9, and they're shorter.

## Which surah should you start with?

Start with the shortest ones. At three or four verses, a whole surah is within easy reach.

That's the order Nūr follows. Its memorisation path begins with al-Fātiḥah, the opening surah of the Quran, which isn't part of Juz Amma. After that come:

- al-Ikhlāṣ (112), four verses. The Prophet ﷺ said it is equal to a third of the Quran (narrated by al-Bukhārī, no. 5013);
- al-Falaq (113);
- an-Nās (114);
- al-Kawthar (108), three verses;
- al-Fīl (105);
- al-Masad (111), an-Naṣr (110), al-Kāfirūn (109), al-Māʿūn (107), then Quraysh (106).The path then resumes at al-Humazah (104) and works backwards through the Quran, one surah at a time. It finishes Juz Amma with an-Naba (78), then continues with surah 77 and the rest of the Quran.

Longer surahs are split into passages of a few verses. An-Naba, for example, is memorised in seven passages. You hear each passage recited by al-Ḥuṣarī, read along with him, then read it on your own. Next you recite it from memory, and Nūr shows you which word to repeat. Revision then brings back what you know at longer and longer intervals, so it stays with you.

If you're still learning to read, you'll meet these five surahs early on, in the reading lessons: al-Fātiḥah, al-Ikhlāṣ, al-Falaq, an-Nās and al-Kawthar.

And if a surah is a struggle, remember what the Prophet ﷺ said: whoever recites the Quran with difficulty receives a double reward (narrated by al-Bukhārī, no. 4937, and Muslim, no. 798).

## The stories behind the surahs

Several surahs in Juz Amma come with a story: the events around them, or what the Prophet ﷺ and his companions said about them. Nūr tells some of these stories, for you to read and listen to, in English and French. Here are a few.

- al-Fīl , "Held back, like the elephant". On the road to Makkah, the Prophet's ﷺ camel kneels and won't move. He says: "She was stopped by the One who stopped the elephant" (narrated by al-Bukhārī, no. 2731).
- al-Masad , "The call from Ṣafā". The Prophet ﷺ climbs a hill in Makkah to warn his people.
- Quraysh , "Winter and summer". The caravans of the Quraysh tribe, with one journey in winter and another in summer.
- az-Zalzalah , "An atom's weight". A verse in which every deed counts, even the smallest.
- al-Kawthar , "The river he smiled about". Anas describes the day this surah was revealed.
- an-Nās , "Three surahs at bedtime". ʿĀʾishah describes what the Prophet ﷺ recited before he went to sleep.To get started, open the Memorise section in Nūr: al-Fātiḥah comes first, then Juz Amma in the order above.

# Arabic Alphabet: the 28 Letters for Reading the Quran

URL: https://getnurapp.com/en/blog/arabic-alphabet-28-letters/
Language: en

The Arabic alphabet has 28 letters. It reads from right to left, and most letters join on to the next one. Below are all 28 with their names, followed by what you need to know before you read a page of the Quran.

## How many letters are in the Arabic alphabet: 28 or 29?

There are 28. That's the usual count, and the one you get when you recite the alphabet in order.

Some lists give 29 because they add the hamzah (ء). The hamzah is a catch in the throat, like the break in "uh-oh". It's written on its own or sits on an alif, a wāw or a yāʾ. Both counts describe the same script.

Here are the 28 letters in alphabetical order, with their names as Nūr spells them.

| No. | Letter | Name |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | ا | Alif |
| 2 | ب | Bā |
| 3 | ت | Tā |
| 4 | ث | Thā |
| 5 | ج | Jīm |
| 6 | ح | Ḥā |
| 7 | خ | Khā |
| 8 | د | Dāl |
| 9 | ذ | Dhāl |
| 10 | ر | Rā |
| 11 | ز | Zāy |
| 12 | س | Sīn |
| 13 | ش | Shīn |
| 14 | ص | Ṣād |
| 15 | ض | Ḍād |
| 16 | ط | Ṭā |
| 17 | ظ | Ẓā |
| 18 | ع | ʿAyn |
| 19 | غ | Ghayn |
| 20 | ف | Fā |
| 21 | ق | Qāf |
| 22 | ك | Kāf |
| 23 | ل | Lām |
| 24 | م | Mīm |
| 25 | ن | Nūn |
| 26 | ه | Hā |
| 27 | و | Wāw |
| 28 | ي | Yā |

In these names, a dot under a letter, as in Ḥā or Ṣād, marks a sound English doesn't have. Ḥā is a breathy h, from deep in the throat. Ṣād is a heavy s, said with a full mouth.

## Why a letter changes shape at the start, middle and end of a word

In Arabic, the letters of a word are joined together. Every page of the Quran is written like this. So each letter can take up to four shapes: on its own, at the start of a word, in the middle or at the end.

Take ب, Bā:

- on its own: ب ;
- at the start: بـ ;
- in the middle: ـبـ ;
- at the end: ـب .The joining stroke shows which side the letter connects on. The dots never change: same number, same place. In the middle of a word, five letters even share the same body: ب ت ث ن ي. Only the dots tell them apart. Check the dots and you'll know which letter it is.

Six letters never join the letter after them: ا د ذ ر ز و. After one of these, there's a gap in the word: the next letter isn't joined to it.

## Where are the vowels? Marks above and below the letters

The 28 letters mostly stand for consonants. Short vowels are written as marks above or below the letter:

- fatḥah , a stroke above, is read as a: بَ , ba;
- kasrah , a stroke below, is read as i: بِ , bi;
- ḍammah , a wāw-shaped mark above, is read as u: بُ , bu.A few other marks complete the picture. **Sukūn** means there's no vowel: the letter closes the syllable. **Shaddah** doubles the letter. **Tanwīn** doubles the vowel and adds an n.

Every one of these marks is written in the Quran, so you never have to guess how a word sounds. Take its first word, بِسۡمِ: a b with kasrah, an s with sukūn and an m with kasrah. It's read "bismi".

Three letters also act as long vowels: alif for a long a, wāw for a long u and yāʾ for a long i.

## How to learn the Arabic alphabet easily

- Learn each letter's name and its sound. ب is called Bā. With a fatḥah, it's pronounced ba. They're two different things, and you need both.
- Listen before you read. Some sounds don't exist in English. ح is a breathy h, from deep in the throat. ق is a k made far back in the throat. ع is a deep sound from the middle of the throat. A written description can get you close, and your ear does the rest.
- Start with the letters of the Basmalah. The order of the alphabet isn't the order to learn it in. Nūr starts with the ten letters of the Basmalah, the line that opens the Quran: ا ل م ه ب س ن ي ر ح . The rest follow according to how often they appear in the Quran, with each hard sound coming after its easier counterpart.
- Read a real word early on. Once you know alif, lām and hā, you can already spot the word ٱللَّهِ , Allah, in the Basmalah.
- Group the letters that look alike. ج ح خ share the same body, and so do س ش . Learn them side by side, and watch where the dots go.
- Come back to it every day, even for a few minutes. Review the letters you already know, not just the new ones.

> "Whoever reads a letter of the Book of Allah receives a good deed, and a good deed is worth ten. I do not say that alif lām mīm is one letter. Alif is a letter, lām is a letter, mīm is a letter." The Prophet ﷺ, in a hadith reported by at-Tirmidhī, no. 2910.

Those three letters open Surah al-Baqarah: الٓمٓ. Every letter you read in the Quran counts. And if you're slow at first, the Prophet ﷺ also said that someone who finds reciting the Quran difficult receives a double reward (reported by al-Bukhārī, no. 4937, and Muslim, no. 798).

## Do you need to speak Arabic to read the Quran?

No. Reading the Quran means recognising the letters and marks and saying the sounds they stand for. Understanding Arabic as a language is a separate skill. Many Muslims read the Quran aloud without speaking Arabic, and turn to a translation for its meaning.

Nūr teaches you to read the Quran. It doesn't teach the Arabic language. The Read section has four stages: the letters, joined letters, the marks, then the page of the Quran. While you learn the letters, you hear al-Fātiḥah recited one verse at a time by al-Ḥuṣarī. By the end, you can read al-Fātiḥah and al-Ikhlāṣ from the page of the muṣḥaf, the written copy of the Quran, without any help.

To begin with the first letter, open the Read section in Nūr.

# How to Read the Quran as an Adult Beginner

URL: https://getnurapp.com/en/blog/how-to-read-the-quran-adult-beginner/
Language: en

To learn to read the Quran from scratch, take it in this order: the letters, the vowels, the words, then a verse on the page. If you’ve never read a letter of Arabic, you have nothing to unlearn. Each step builds on the one before.

## Can you learn to read the Quran on your own?

Yes. Here, reading means recognising the Arabic letters and saying the words out loud. You can start on your own and go at your own pace. What you need most is a clear order to follow, and a recitation to listen to so you can hear every sound. Understanding Arabic as a language is a separate skill, and you don’t need it to read.

Having a teacher listen to you read is still a real help. People often learn tajwīd, the finer rules of recitation, later on with a teacher. But you don’t need to wait for one to take your first steps.

If you stumble over every word, don’t worry. The Prophet ﷺ spoke of two kinds of reader. The one who reads the Quran with ease is with the noble and righteous angels. About the other, he said:

> “The one who stumbles as they read the Quran, and finds it hard, will have two rewards.”

Muslim records this hadith (no. 798), and al-Bukhārī records one with a similar meaning (no. 4937). The very first word of the Quran to be revealed was “Read” (reported by al-Bukhārī, no. 3). The verse means: Read, in the name of your Lord who created.

Here are the four steps, in order:

- The letters , one at a time, each with its sound.

- The vowels , the marks that turn a letter into a syllable.

- The words , made of letters joined together.

- A verse , read straight from the page of the Quran.

## Where to start: the letters

Start with the alphabet. It has 28 letters, and our article on the Arabic alphabet goes through them one by one. Arabic is read from right to left.

Each letter has a name and a sound. ب is called bā’, and it makes a b sound. When you read, it’s the sound that matters.

Don’t try to learn them all at once. Take one letter, listen to its sound and look at its shape. Once you can recognise it without hesitating, move on to the next. Each day, review yesterday’s letters first.

Some letters differ only in their dots. ب (bā’) has one dot below, ت (tā’) has two above and ث (thā’) has three. The dots tell you which letter you’re looking at. It’s normal to mix them up at first.

A few sounds don’t exist in English, such as ع (ʿayn) and ح (ḥā’). Listen to them often before you try to say them. Your ear learns them first, and your voice follows.

## Reading words: joined letters and vowel marks

A letter on its own can’t be read yet. It needs a vowel: a mark written above or below it. The fatḥah, a stroke above the letter, gives an a sound. The kasrah, a stroke below, gives i. The ḍammah, a loop above, gives u. With these three marks, you can read your first syllables: ba, bi, bu.

Next come words. Within a word, the letters join together, and each one changes shape slightly depending on where it sits: at the start, in the middle or at the end. Six letters never join the letter after them, such as ا (alif) and د (dāl). That’s why a single word can have gaps in it.

You’ll see a few other marks all the time. The sukūn, written above a letter, shows that it has no vowel. The shaddah, which looks like a w, shows that the letter is said twice. The tanwīn, a vowel written twice at the end of a word, adds an n sound: ban, bin, bun.

Start with short words of two or three letters. Read them slowly and out loud, one syllable at a time.

## Reading the page of the Quran without transliteration

Transliteration is Arabic written in the Latin alphabet, like “Bismi llāhi”. It helps you keep up at the beginning. But several Arabic sounds have no English letter, so transliteration can only get close to them. What you want to read is the Arabic text itself, so put transliteration aside as soon as you can.

A page of the Quran uses the letters and vowels you already know, plus a few extra marks, such as the one that lengthens a sound. Each verse ends with a circle with its number inside. Pick a verse you’ve heard many times, like the first verse of al-Fātiḥah, the surah that opens the Quran. Listen to it word by word, then read it on your own.

At first you’ll recognise single letters, then whole words. This verse means: In the name of Allah, the All-Merciful, the Ever-Merciful.

## How long should you read each day?

A few minutes a day, at the same time if you can. Reading every day matters more than reading for a long time. Link your session to a moment that’s already part of your day, such as a break or a bus ride.

A short session can follow the same pattern every time. First, reread what you learned the day before. Then add just one new thing: a letter, a vowel or a word. Always read aloud, even if quietly. Stop while it still feels easy, and pick it up again the next day.

Nobody can tell you how many weeks it will take before you can read the page. Everyone learns at their own pace. The day you open the page and read it by yourself, you’ll know why you started.

In Nūr, the Read door goes letter by letter, until you can read al-Fātiḥah and al-Ikhlāṣ from the page of the Quran, unaided.

---

# How to Memorise the Quran Without Forgetting It

URL: https://getnurapp.com/en/blog/how-to-memorize-the-quran-without-forgetting/
Language: en

To hold on to what you’ve memorised, revise it: the next day, then at longer and longer intervals. Each day, revise before you learn anything new. Everyone forgets, and what you revise falls back into place.

## Why we forget what we’ve memorised

Memory holds on to what gets used. A passage you recite once and then set aside slowly fades. A passage you come back to often eventually stays with you on its own. This happens to everyone, even after years of memorising.

The Prophet ﷺ described this with an image from his own time. Someone who knows the Quran by heart is like the owner of hobbled camels: if he keeps watch over them, he holds on to them, and if he lets them loose, they wander off (reported by al-Bukhārī, no. 5031, and Muslim, no. 789). The image simply shows how it works: what you look after stays with you.

Did you learn some surahs years ago and now only remember parts of them? As a rule, relearning something you once knew is faster than learning it the first time.

## Revise at longer and longer intervals

The idea is simple: return to a passage before it fades, then leave a slightly longer gap before the next time. For example:

- On the day you learn it, recite it one last time before you finish.
- The next day.
- Three days later.
- A week later.
- Then after two weeks, then after a month.Each time, recite from memory before you open the text, then check. If it’s all there, you can wait longer before the next round. If a word has slipped, come back sooner. Digging a word out of your memory, even when it’s hard, makes it stick better than rereading it.

One feeling can mislead you. When you recognise a passage as you hear it, it feels as if you know it. The real test is reciting it with no audio and no text.

## Balancing new memorisation and revision

One simple rule: revision first, new material second. In each session, work in this order:

- Revise older passages : the ones due for revision today.
- Recite yesterday’s passage , linked to the one before it.
- Learn today’s passage.The more surahs you know, the more time revision takes. That’s a good sign: you have more to look after. If it gets too much, slow down on new passages for a few days. Holding on to what you know matters as much as learning more.

Make a note of the passages that often slip, and give them extra revision. Often these are the joins between two passages, and verses that look alike across different surahs.

To learn today’s passage, follow the method in How to Memorise a Surah Fast and Keep It.

> Revision first, new material second.

## How long does it take to memorise the whole Quran?

It depends on your pace, and the maths is simple. The Medina muṣḥaf, a printed edition of the Quran, has 604 pages. The Quran has 114 surahs and 6,236 verses.

- One page a day : 604 days, about a year and eight months.
- Half a page a day : about three years and four months.
- A quarter of a page a day : about six years and seven months.These figures only count new pages. Revision-only days, busy days and breaks add to the total. They’re just calculations. Your real pace depends on your life, and a slow pace kept up every day eventually covers the whole Quran.

You can also aim to learn one part before the whole. Juzʾ ʿAmma (Juz Amma), the last of the Quran’s 30 parts, contains 37 surahs, many of them short. That’s where Nūr starts, after al-Fātiḥah.

## Memorising with only a little time each day

A few minutes a day go further than one long session a week. Tie your session to a set time of day: after your morning coffee, on the bus, before you go to sleep.

Listen to today’s passage while you’re travelling. Recite it in your head as you walk. On busy days, just revise: you hold on to what you have, and the new passage can wait until tomorrow.

A short passage is enough. Three verses you know well are worth more than ten you half know.

And the Quran is meant to be remembered. In Surah al-Qamar, Allah says: وَلَقَدۡ يَسَّرۡنَا ٱلۡقُرۡءَانَ لِلذِّكۡرِ فَهَلۡ مِن مُّدَّكِرࣲ‏ (54:17). It means: “We have made the Quran easy to remember. Is there anyone who will remember?”

## What the Prophet ﷺ said about revision

The Prophet ﷺ told people to return to the Quran regularly. He swore that it slips from memory faster than camels break free of their hobbles. Al-Bukhārī (no. 5033) and Muslim (no. 791) both report it.

The word he used, taʿāhadū, means coming back to something regularly to look after it. It’s practical advice. It tells you how to hold on to the Quran: come back to it a little, and often.

In Nūr, the Memorise section brings back what you’ve memorised at the right time, so it stays with you.

---

# Story of Surah Al Fil and the Year of the Elephant

URL: https://getnurapp.com/en/blog/story-of-surah-al-fil/
Language: en

Surah Al-Fīl, “The Elephant”, is only five verses long. It tells how Allah held back men who moved against Makkah with an elephant. This article covers what the surah says, what the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ himself said about it, and what it leaves out.

## What is Surah Al Fil about?

A surah is a chapter of the Quran. Al-Fīl is surah 105, one of the shortest. It’s part of Juz Amma, the last of the Quran’s thirty parts.

The surah is about “the people of the elephant”. These were men who headed for Makkah, a city in Arabia, bringing an elephant with them. In the middle of the city stands the Kaʿbah, a stone building known as the House of Allah. The Quran doesn’t say who these men were. Scholars who wrote commentaries on the Quran say they had come to destroy the Kaʿbah.

Allah didn’t let them do it. He sent flock after flock of birds against them, pelting them with stones. Their plan came to nothing, and the Kaʿbah stood unharmed.

Years later, on the day he entered Makkah, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ spoke of it himself. He praised Allah, then told the people: “Allah held back the elephant from Makkah.” Al-Bukhārī (no. 2434) and Muslim (no. 1355) both record this saying. Each compiled a collection of hadiths, the sayings and acts of the Prophet ﷺ, and scholars hold these collections to be authentic.

The surah opens with a question to the Prophet ﷺ: have you not seen what your Lord did? According to the commentator as-Saʿdī, the story shows Allah’s power and His mercy towards His servants.

## The five verses in English

Below, each verse is given in Arabic, followed by its meaning in plain English. The meaning helps you follow the text, but it’s no substitute for a full translation.

أَلَمۡ تَرَ كَيۡفَ فَعَلَ رَبُّكَ بِأَصۡحَٰبِ ٱلۡفِيلِ

**1.** Have you not seen what your Lord did with the people of the elephant?

أَلَمۡ يَجۡعَلۡ كَيۡدَهُمۡ فِي تَضۡلِيلࣲ‏

**2.** Did He not turn their scheming into nothing?

وَأَرۡسَلَ عَلَيۡهِمۡ طَيۡرًا أَبَابِيلَ

**3.** And He sent flocks of birds against them

تَرۡمِيهِم بِحِجَارَةࣲ مِّن سِجِّيلࣲ‏

**4.** Pelting them with stones of baked clay

فَجَعَلَهُمۡ كَعَصۡفࣲ مَّأۡكُولِۭ

**5.** And left them like straw that has been chewed up

Three words are worth explaining. Their “scheming” is the plan the people of the elephant made against the Kaʿbah. The word أَبَابِيلَ, abābīl, means groups of birds arriving one after another, as Ibn ʿAbbās explained. The chewed-up straw is an image: nothing was left of their strength.

These verses are short. If you’d like to learn them by heart, you’ll find the method in How to memorise a surah fast and keep it.

## Why it is called the Year of the Elephant

The event left such a mark on Makkah that the year it happened became known as “the Year of the Elephant”.

It’s also the year the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was born. Ibn ʿAbbās, a Companion of the Prophet ﷺ, put it in a single sentence: “The Prophet ﷺ was born in the Year of the Elephant.” A Companion is someone who knew him and followed him. Al-Ḥākim records this report in his collection al-Mustadrak (no. 4225), and the book’s editors grade its chain of narration “good” (ḥasan). A chain of narration is the line of people who passed a saying on, one after another.

The reliable reports don’t say whether he was born before or after the elephant came. They only say it was the same year.

This means the Prophet ﷺ didn’t see the elephant with his own eyes. When the surah asks him “have you not seen”, the commentator aṭ-Ṭabarī takes it to mean seeing with the heart. In other words: have you not understood what your Lord did?

## “The One who held back the elephant”: the surah in the life of the Prophet ﷺ

The Prophet ﷺ mentioned the elephant in another story too, which al-Bukhārī records in his collection (nos. 2731 and 4178). It took place a few years before he entered Makkah.

More than a thousand Companions set out with him for Makkah. They wanted to perform ʿumrah, a visit to the Kaʿbah, and they meant to do it in peace. The Prophet ﷺ made it clear that they hadn’t come to fight anyone. But the leaders of Makkah, who still opposed Islam, meant to stop them, even if it came to a fight.

At a mountain pass near the city, the Prophet’s ﷺ camel, al-Qaṣwāʾ, knelt down and wouldn’t get up again. People said, “She is being stubborn.” The Prophet ﷺ replied: “She is not stubborn, that is not her nature. But the One who held back the elephant has held her back.”

> “The One who held back the elephant has held her back.”

Ibn Ḥajar, a scholar who wrote a commentary on al-Bukhārī’s collection, explains the link. Allah was holding the Muslims back from Makkah, just as He had held back the elephant. If they had forced their way in, fighting would have broken out in the sacred city. In both stories, Allah protected Makkah.

The Prophet ﷺ then swore that he would accept any proposal from the leaders of Makkah that honoured the sacred things of Allah. He urged his camel on, and she leapt to her feet. The Muslims made camp at al-Ḥudaybiyah, a place near Makkah, and a peace treaty was drawn up with the city’s leaders. Under it, the Muslims could come back and visit the Kaʿbah the following year.

Another scholar, al-Khaṭṭābī, explains what the Prophet ﷺ meant. In this case, honouring the sacred things of Allah meant giving up the fight and choosing peace. Ibn Ḥajar also lists this hadith under Surah Al-Fīl.

The Prophet ﷺ chose peace over a fight. That peace opened the way to the Kaʿbah for the Muslims.

## What the surah does not say

The surah doesn’t name the people of the elephant or their leader. It doesn’t describe the birds or the stones, and it gives no date. Many retellings give a much longer version, with a king’s name, his reasons and the details of his march. That version comes mostly from Ibn Isḥāq, an eighth-century historian who doesn’t say where he heard it. The descriptions of the birds come from men born long after the event, and they name no witness. There are other reports about the Year of the Elephant, but hadith specialists grade their chains as weak. This article leaves them out. It sticks to the five verses and to the sayings of the Prophet ﷺ that are held to be authentic.

In the Nūr app, you’ll find the story of the kneeling camel in the Stories, under the title “Held back, like the elephant”.

---

# Story of Prophet Yusuf, as the Quran Tells It

URL: https://getnurapp.com/en/blog/story-of-prophet-yusuf/
Language: en

Surah Yusuf, the twelfth chapter of the Quran, tells a single story across 111 verses: the story of the Prophet Yūsuf, known in the Bible as Joseph. Just before it begins, the Quran says to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: “We tell you the most beautiful of stories.”

## The dream of the eleven stars

Yūsuf was a young boy. His father, Yaʿqūb, known in the Bible as Jacob, was also a prophet. Yūsuf told him about a dream.

إِذۡ قَالَ يُوسُفُ لِأَبِيهِ يَٰٓأَبَتِ إِنِّي رَأَيۡتُ أَحَدَ عَشَرَ كَوۡكَبࣰا وَٱلشَّمۡسَ وَٱلۡقَمَرَ رَأَيۡتُهُمۡ لِي سَٰجِدِينَ

“Father, I saw eleven stars, and the sun and the moon, bow down to the ground before me.”

Yaʿqūb replied: “Do not tell your dream to your brothers, or they may plot against you.” He added that Allah would choose him and teach him how to interpret dreams (12:6).

The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ described this family in these words: “The noble, son of the noble, son of the noble, son of the noble: Yūsuf, son of Yaʿqūb, son of Isḥāq, son of Ibrāhīm” (al-Bukhārī, no. 3390). Isḥāq is Isaac, and Ibrāhīm is Abraham. Al-Bukhārī’s book is a collection of hadiths, the sayings of the Prophet ﷺ, which scholars hold to be authentic.

## The well and the shirt

Yūsuf had other brothers, and they were jealous: “Yūsuf and his brother are dearer to our father than we are.” The brother they mention was another son of Yaʿqūb. The surah doesn’t name him. Some of them wanted to kill Yūsuf. One suggested putting him in a well instead, where travellers would find him (12:10).

The brothers talked Yaʿqūb into letting Yūsuf go out with them to run and play, although he was afraid a wolf might eat the boy (12:11-13). They lowered him to the bottom of a well. There, Allah made this known to him: “One day you will tell them what they did, and they will not know it is you.”

That evening the brothers came home in tears, carrying his shirt stained with false blood. A wolf had eaten him, they said. Yaʿqūb didn’t believe them: “No, you have talked yourselves into a wrong deed. What is left to me is beautiful patience, and Allah is the One I ask for help.” Beautiful patience, the commentators explain, means staying calm and not complaining to people.

Some travellers came by the well. One of them lowered his bucket and called out: “Good news! Here is a boy!” They took Yūsuf and sold him for a few coins (12:20).

## The house of the ʿAzīz, then prison

In Egypt, a high official bought Yūsuf. The surah calls him the ʿAzīz, “the mighty one”. Yūsuf grew up in his house, and Allah gave him wisdom and knowledge (12:21-22).

The ʿAzīz’s wife tried to seduce him. She shut the doors, but Yūsuf refused: “I seek refuge in Allah!” He ran for the door. She caught hold of him, and his shirt tore at the back. Then, in front of her husband, she accused Yūsuf. A man from her own family settled the matter: the tear at the back showed that Yūsuf was telling the truth. Her husband believed Yūsuf (12:25-29).

The women of the city began to gossip. The ʿAzīz’s wife invited them and called Yūsuf in. When they saw him, they cut their hands with their knives: “This is no human being. This is a noble angel!”

The ʿAzīz’s wife threatened him with prison. Yūsuf said to Allah: “My Lord, prison is dearer to me than what they ask of me.” He was locked up, even though they knew he was innocent (12:32-35).

In prison, two young men told him their dreams. He spoke to them first about Allah, the One who alone deserves worship, and then interpreted their dreams (12:36-41). He asked the one who was about to be freed to mention him to the king. But Satan made the man forget, and Yūsuf stayed in prison for several years (12:42).

## The king’s dream and the years of famine

The king of Egypt dreamt of seven fat cows being eaten by seven thin ones, and of seven green ears of grain beside seven dry ones (12:43). No one could interpret it. Then the man who had been freed from prison remembered Yūsuf (12:45).

Yūsuf explained what the dream meant. Seven years of good harvests were coming, and the grain should be left in the ear. Seven hard years would follow, when people would live on those stores. Then a year of rain would bring relief (12:47-49).

The king sent for him, but Yūsuf wanted his innocence made clear first (12:50). The Prophet ﷺ praised this patience: “Had I stayed in prison as long as Yūsuf stayed, I would have answered the one who called me” (al-Bukhārī, no. 3372, and Muslim, no. 151).

The ʿAzīz’s wife confessed: “It was I who tried to seduce him, and he is telling the truth.” The king made him his close adviser. Later, at Yūsuf’s own request, he put him in charge of the country’s storehouses (12:54-56).

## His brothers come back: “No blame on you today”

During the hard years, Yaʿqūb’s sons came to Egypt to buy grain. Yūsuf recognised them, but they didn’t recognise him (12:58). He asked them to come back with the brother who had stayed at home with their father (12:59).

Yaʿqūb hesitated, having already lost Yūsuf, but in the end he agreed (12:64-66). In Egypt, Yūsuf took this brother aside and told him: “I am your brother. Do not be sad.” Then he had the king’s cup hidden in his brother’s bag. By the brothers’ own rule, whoever had the cup had to stay behind. In this way, Yūsuf kept his brother with him (12:70-76).

The others went home without him. Once again Yaʿqūb met the news with beautiful patience (12:83), but his grief for Yūsuf turned his eyes white (12:84). He said: “I complain of my grief to Allah alone.” Then he sent his sons back to look for Yūsuf and his brother, and he never lost hope in Allah’s mercy (12:87).

When the brothers stood before Yūsuf in Egypt once more, he asked them what they had done to Yūsuf and his brother (12:89). The truth dawned on them: “Are you Yūsuf?” He answered: “I am Yūsuf, and this is my brother.” They admitted they had done wrong (12:91), and Yūsuf said to them:

قَالَ لَا تَثۡرِيبَ عَلَيۡكُمُ ٱلۡيَوۡمَۖ يَغۡفِرُ ٱللَّهُ لَكُمۡۖ وَهُوَ أَرۡحَمُ ٱلرَّٰحِمِينَ

“No blame on you today. May Allah forgive you. He is the most merciful of all who show mercy.”

He gave them his shirt to take to their father. When it was laid over Yaʿqūb’s face, his sight returned (12:93-96). His sons asked him to seek Allah’s forgiveness for them, and he promised he would (12:97-98).

The whole family came to Egypt. Yūsuf seated his parents on the throne, and they all bowed before him. The commentators say this was a greeting of respect at the time. Yūsuf said: “Father, this is the meaning of my dream of long ago.” The eleven stars were his brothers, and the sun and the moon were his parents.

In that moment of joy, Yūsuf mentioned the prison, but not the well. He said only that Satan had caused a rift “between me and my brothers”. The commentator as-Saʿdī sees this as complete forgiveness, without a single word of reproach.

## What the surah does not say

The surah doesn’t name Yūsuf’s brothers or the ʿAzīz’s wife. It doesn’t give Yūsuf’s age, the colour of his shirt or how long he spent in the well. The names and details you may read elsewhere come from later accounts that can’t be traced back to any reliable witness. This article keeps to the Quran and to authentic hadiths, and so does our article on the story of Surah Al-Fīl.

In the Nūr app, the Stories tell one part of this surah: the dream, the well and the shirt. You’ll find it under the title “The shirt and the wolf”.
